articles.title: FPOA Honors SJAA With Free Food At The Peak d'editor
articles.summary: The Fremont Peak Observatory Association (FPOA) is honoring the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) with an "Appreciation Night" on September 18th. This event will feature free food, including hamburgers and hot dogs, followed by an opportunity for members to observe through the 30-inch Challenger telescope. The gathering is scheduled for a virtually moonless night, providing an excellent observing opportunity and a chance for club members to socialize and celebrate their contributions.

articles.title: SJAA Activities Calendar
articles.summary: This document outlines the San Jose Astronomical Association's (SJAA) activity calendar for September and October, detailing numerous events such as star parties at Houge Park and Fremont Peak, astronomy classes on astrophotography and CCD imaging, and a general meeting featuring speaker Peter Jenniskens. It also includes special events like a Yosemite Weekend and 'SJAA Appreciation Night'. The calendar provides practical information including sunset and moon phases, contact details, and a note about insurance coverage for members.

articles.title: Loaner Program Plans
articles.summary: SJAA is planning significant improvements and expansions for its Loaner Program, a key activity for the organization. Under the direction of Mike Koop, the initiative aims to upgrade the current telescope inventory by adding star charts and eyepieces, and acquire new equipment such as a quality refractor, CCD setup, LX-200, and a truss-tube dobsonian. The organization will be instituting fundraising activities to finance these enhancements and seeking assistance for scope repairs.

articles.title: Web Ephemeris Option
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association is offering members the option to switch from receiving a physical paper copy of their Ephemeris to viewing it exclusively on the web. This initiative aims to minimize costs by removing those who don't use the paper version from the postal mailing list. Members who prefer the web option are asked to email the Treasurer to update their mailing status.

articles.title: Preliminary Minutes of the August 8 Meeting of the SJAA Board of Directors
articles.summary: The SJAA Board of Directors convened on August 8 to discuss various club matters, including approving event schedules, reviewing the 1999 calendar (noting a need for an astronomy class teacher), and addressing new trees at the Houge Park observing area. Key decisions involved establishing a fund for acquiring new loaner telescopes and a 'adopt a scope' program, and authorizing an Astronomical Pocket Diary project despite contention over non-astronomical entries. A notable policy change to sell items at a profit, with proceeds funding the loaner program, was also mentioned.

articles.title: July Board Meeting Notes
articles.summary: The July Board Meeting addressed the distribution of the Ephemeris, with plans to investigate electronic options to reduce mailing costs. The board also agreed to establish a fund for acquiring new equipment for the loaner program and discussed creating recruiting business cards. Key updates included a donation of a slide projector and progress on moving the C11 telescope to Fremont Peak.

articles.title: Akkana Peck
articles.summary: This article outlines celestial observing opportunities for late August and September, including Mercury's morning visibility, a close Mars-Beehive cluster pass, and a subtle penumbral lunar eclipse. Key events include Jupiter reaching a close opposition, Saturn's increasingly open rings, and close approaches by asteroids Ceres and Pallas, providing a comprehensive guide for amateur astronomers.

articles.title: Mooning
articles.summary: This article provides an observing guide for the Moon during September, detailing optimal times to view features like the Copernicus crater and its secondary impacts, particularly near the first and last quarters. It highlights the Harvest Moon on the 6th and notes that the third quarter Moon on the 14th will be at its highest for observation. Additionally, it mentions a close encounter between Aldebaran, Ceres, and the Moon on the 11th, along with numerous lesser occultations in a rich star field.

articles.title: Meteor Watch
articles.summary: The article begins with a forecast for the Alpha Aurigids meteor shower, detailing its expected peak around August 31-September 1 with potential for bright meteors from Auriga and its likely origin from Comet Kiess. The second part presents the 1999 SJAA Events Calendar, listing dates for general meetings, astronomy classes, and various star parties. It also includes important notes on moon conditions for observing, event specifics, and other key dates relevant to the astronomy club.

articles.title: Editor's Extras
articles.summary: This 'Editor's Extras' article covers several updates for the SJAA club, noting significant improvements to the Science Center, including a new planetarium. It clarifies that the club is financially sound and encourages members to continue receiving paper copies of the Ephemeris for prompt delivery. A key focus is the push to upgrade and expand the acclaimed loaner telescope program, with an appeal for financial contributions and volunteer support.

articles.title: Activities Through Other Clubs
articles.summary: This article outlines astronomical activities organized by other clubs, encouraging SJAA members to participate. TAC offers indefinite Wednesday evening observing sessions at the Montebello site (weather permitting, permit holder required), while PAS hosts public viewing at Foothill Observatory on clear Friday evenings and solar viewing on clear Saturday mornings. Additionally, PAS has general and board meetings scheduled for September and October at Foothill College.

articles.title: Owooooo!!
articles.summary: An amateur astronomer recounts his detailed naked-eye observations of the nearly full Moon in August 1998, identifying numerous lunar features like major maria and specific craters. He speculates that observing from an illuminated environment, which narrows the pupils, might enhance perceived detail, and discusses the physiological limits of human vision. The author humorously concludes by noting his lack of werewolf transformation despite intense staring.

articles.title: On Zoom Eyepieces:
articles.summary: The author reviews a Vixen 8-24mm zoom eyepiece, noting its superior performance compared to other zoom units, particularly its wider apparent and actual field of view. Contrary to common perceptions of zoom eyepieces, this unit delivered good image quality and proved exceptionally useful for deep-sky objects, allowing quick adjustments to find optimal magnifications for revealing specific features, an "enormous and unexpected win."

articles.title: Tourist, continued from Page 4.
articles.summary: The author shares a highly positive initial experience with the Vixen 8-24mm zoom eyepiece, finding it a convenient and cost-effective substitute for multiple conventional eyepieces during deep-sky observing. While needing further testing, the author tentatively recommends it to other deep-sky observers for potentially better views with less effort and cost. Concerns include its performance at shorter focal ratios and moderate field width for users without driven telescopes.

articles.title: On Skunks:
articles.summary: The author recounts a peaceful several-hour observation session at Coulter Camp in Fremont Peak State Park, California, where they coexisted within 10 meters of a foraging skunk. Both the author and the animal minded their own business, leading the author to appreciate the skunk's good company during the solitary experience.

articles.title: On Local Dwarves:
articles.summary: This article details the visual observation of low-surface-brightness dwarf galaxies, highlighting the challenges and successes of amateur astronomers using various telescopes and binoculars. It provides specific examples of observable dwarf galaxies like NGC 6822, Sculptor, Leo I, Fornax, Andromeda I, II, III, and Leo II, along with the apertures and conditions required to spot them. The author also notes historical observations by figures like Barnard, emphasizing that even professional astronomers faced difficulties.

articles.title: Why Observe the Deep Sky?
articles.summary: This article discusses the compelling reasons for engaging in deep-sky observing as an amateur astronomer. While acknowledging the subjective nature of hobbies, it highlights several pragmatic advantages of deep-sky work over other forms of observing, such as reduced dependence on perfect seeing conditions and less demanding telescope requirements. It also notes the abundance of deep-sky objects available year-round, unlike the seasonal availability of planets.

articles.title: Olivarez On Jupiter
articles.summary: The article reports on a talk by Jose Olivarez from the Chabot Observatory about observing Jupiter, presented at an SJAA meeting. Olivarez discussed fascinating CCD images, planetary sketches, and recent activity on Jupiter, including the Great Red Spot's collision and changes in white ovals. The article also promotes an upcoming 'Planet Watch Workshop' at Chabot, featuring expert speakers like Donald Parker and observing opportunities.

articles.title: Comet Comments
articles.summary: The SOHO satellite, recently located, is unlikely to return useful data after detecting two new sungrazing comets. In other comet news, Comet Meunier-Dupouy and Periodic Comet Giacobini-Zinner are becoming visible in the evening sky, while Comet Linear stays north. The author also shares personal comet hunting statistics, having recorded his 10,000th telescopic meteor and noting an increasing rate of artificial satellite sightings that now exceed meteor rates.

articles.title: Ephemerides - Epoch 2000, 0h UTC
articles.summary: This document provides ephemerides for three comets: C/1997 J2 (Meunier-Dupouy), 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, and C/1998 M5 (Linear). The tables list observational data including Right Ascension, Declination, elongation from the Sun, sky quadrant, and apparent magnitude for various dates in September and October, referenced to Epoch 2000, 0h UTC.

articles.title: Orbital Elements -- Epoch 2000.0
articles.summary: This document presents a table of orbital elements for three celestial objects: Giacobini-Zinner, Meunier-Dupouy, and Linear. For each object, parameters such as perihelion date and distance, argument of perihelion, ascending node, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period are provided. All data is referenced to Epoch 2000.0.

articles.title: Lunar time
articles.summary: This document presents a schedule of key lunar phases for a specific period, including the Full Moon, Last Quarter, New Moon, and First Quarter. For each phase, it provides the precise time in PDT, the date, and the corresponding rise, transit, and set times.

articles.title: Mercury
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for the planet Mercury, detailing its celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), rise, transit, and set times for three specific dates. It also includes Mercury's distance from Earth in AU and its apparent magnitude.

articles.title: Venus
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Venus for specific dates, detailing its distance, apparent magnitude, rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination coordinates. The data is presented in a table format for a period within a month.

articles.title: Mars
articles.summary: This document provides an astronomical ephemeris for Mars, detailing its distance, magnitude, and key observational times for three specific dates within a month. It includes rise, transit, and set times, along with right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec) coordinates, serving as a guide for observers.

articles.title: Jupiter
articles.summary: This document provides an observational guide for Jupiter, detailing its distance, magnitude, and celestial coordinates. It includes specific rise, transit, and set times, along with Right Ascension and Declination, for three distinct dates within a month.

articles.title: Saturn
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris for Saturn, detailing its distance, magnitude, and key observational data for three specific dates. It includes rise, transit, and set times, along with its Right Ascension and Declination, useful for astronomers planning observations.

articles.title: SOL Type G2V Intelligent Life in System ?
articles.summary: This document, identified as an August 1998 ephemeris from SJAA, presents various astronomical tables and data. It includes schedules for hours of darkness, astronomical twilight, and sidereal time across several dates in August and September. Additionally, it details specific celestial events for a 'Darkest Saturday Night' on September 19, 1998, providing sunset, twilight, moonset, and dawn times.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors for an organization. It includes the names of individuals holding positions such as President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and Directors, along with their respective phone numbers. This serves as a directory for the organization's leadership.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: The document 'Ephemeris Staff' lists the key personnel responsible for the publication Ephemeris. It identifies David North as the Editor, Bob Brauer and Lew Kurtz for Circulation, and Accuprint for printing, along with their respective contact phone numbers.

articles.title: Submit
articles.summary: This document encourages members to submit articles for publication in the SJAA Ephemeris. Submissions should be sent via email to Dave North at Timocharis@aol.com.

articles.title: Finding Fremont Peak
articles.summary: This article provides detailed driving directions to Fremont Peak State Park, located south of San Juan Bautista. It guides visitors from Hwy 101 near Gilroy, through specific turns and distances on Hwy G-1, noting a road jog and the park's $3 entrance fee.

articles.title: Telescope Loaner Program Status
articles.summary: The Telescope Loaner Program currently has all its scopes available for any SJAA member. Interested members should contact Mike Koop directly via email or phone to borrow a telescope.

articles.title: Current Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists telescopes currently on loan, specifying the scope's description, the borrower, and the due date. It informs interested parties that they will be placed on a waiting list until a scope becomes available after its due date.

articles.title: Extended Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists astronomical telescopes with extended loan periods available through a lending program. Interested parties can request to borrow one of these scopes, and the organization will coordinate a transfer with the current borrower. The list includes various types of telescopes, their current borrowers, and due dates.

articles.title: Stored Scopes
articles.summary: The 'Stored Scopes' program provides SJAA members with telescopes available for immediate loan, which are stored at other members' homes. Interested members can contact Mike Koop to arrange a pick-up at any listed SJAA event. The article also lists specific scopes available and seeks volunteers for additional storage space.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The 'SJAA Ephemeris', the official newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published monthly throughout the year. The document also provides instructions on how to subscribe to or unsubscribe from the SJAA mailing list via email.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), outlining fees for standard ($15) and junior ($6) memberships, with an optional Sky & Telescope magazine subscription ($27). It provides instructions for new or renewal applications, requiring payment by check to "SJAA" and submission either at an SJAA meeting or via mail to the treasurer, Bob Elsberry, at the provided address and contact information.
